why: Per-problem log-odds move linearly with the share of the sign pattern kept: cue base logit 1.52 (410) plus 0.25 of the 1.01 logit gap to RL (463) gives 85.4 %, so dose is near-linear, not a switch that saturates early.
Same logit-linear dose at a = 0.5: logit 2.02, 88.3 % of 500.
Same logit-linear dose at a = 0.75: logit 2.27, 90.6 % of 500.
The delta is a small first-order shift (0.24 % of norm, 0.36 % at a = 1.5), so extrapolating along the same sign pattern keeps or slightly raises RL's accuracy instead of collapsing.
Plain prompt, logit-linear dose: plain base logit -0.21 (224) plus 0.25 of the 2.74 gap to RL gives 61.7 %, far below a switch-like 375.
Plain prompt, logit-linear dose at a = 0.5: logit 1.16, 76.1 % of 500.
The Code-RL change agrees with the Math-RL signs only at chance, so it carries none of the math sign pattern and the cued model scores like the cued base (410).
Code-RL carries no math sign pattern, so with the plain prompt it stays near the plain base (224).
A random matched-norm difference has no coherent sign pattern and roughly 1/700 of the RL direction's leverage, so it behaves like a reseeded cued base (410).
A random matched-norm difference changes nothing systematic, so mean tokens stay at the cued base's 3,933 within sampling noise rather than moving toward RL's length.
